scenario: A regional bank wants Claude to "make small-business loan pre-qualification decisions" for applications up to $250k. A scorecard validated by model-risk management already produces the decision from 22 structured inputs; analysts spend about 40 minutes per application keying those inputs from tax returns, bank statements, and PDF financials. Adverse-action notices must state the actual factors behind a decline, and any change to the decision logic requires a multi-month revalidation. The bank holds six years of analyst-keyed inputs paired with their source documents.
stem: Select the TWO decisions that best frame and scope the project under these constraints.

options.text: Keep the validated scorecard as the decision-maker, and use Claude to populate its 22 inputs from the source documents, each value carrying a citation to its source for analyst spot-checks.
Have Claude produce the approve or decline recommendation with a written rationale, and reuse that rationale as the adverse-action text so notices read in plain language for applicants.
Define success as field-level agreement with analyst-keyed values on held-out past applications, plus analyst minutes per application, with decisions unchanged for identical inputs.
Pilot Claude auto-declining the applications with the lowest scorecard scores, with analysts sampling the declines, to remove the largest block of manual work in the first quarter.
Add Claude as a second reviewer on scorecard declines, flagging any decline it disagrees with so an analyst can reconsider and override the scorecard result.

rationale.correct: The bottleneck is data entry, not the decision, and the decision logic is validated and expensive to change. Framing Claude as an extractor that feeds the existing scorecard captures the labor saving without touching the validated logic, and the six years of paired inputs and documents make field-level accuracy directly measurable. Success is then defined on extraction agreement and analyst time, with decision parity as a guardrail.

distractors.B: A model-written rationale is not a faithful record of the factors that drove the decision, and it makes Claude the decision-maker, which changes the validated logic and triggers revalidation.
distractors.D: Auto-declining changes the decision process the scorecard was validated for, so it needs revalidation, and the notices would then have to explain Claude's role rather than the scorecard's actual factors.
distractors.E: A second reviewer that can prompt overrides becomes an unvalidated influence on decisions and adds analyst workload instead of removing the keying effort that is the real cost.

scenario:
A software vendor piloted Claude to triage inbound partner support emails into 14 categories so each reaches the right queue. The go/no-go bar was set from an offline evaluation. Week-one figures, where agreement means Claude's category matched the one the human triager assigned:
Offline eval (2,000 emails from last year's labeled archive): agreement 91%
Production week 1 (6,400 emails): agreement 76%
Share labeled "other": archive 9%, production 38%
Production agreement excluding "other": 89%
The archive's few "other" emails are older cases and are not representative of the current traffic.
stem: What does this evidence show about the project's framing, and what should the team do before the go/no-go decision?

options.text: The eval set under-represents the long tail; rebuild the go/no-go measure from a random, triager-labeled sample of live emails, and decide whether "other" needs sub-categories or a human path.
The model is weak on rare categories; add few-shot examples for each of the 14 categories and rerun the offline evaluation until agreement is back at 91%, then launch against the original bar.
Stratify the offline eval by category and reweight it to the production category mix, still drawing from the labeled archive, then rerun the agreement bar on the reweighted result.
The "other" bucket is not a real queue; keep the 91% bar but score production only on the 62% of emails that fall into the 14 named categories, where agreement already meets expectations.

rationale.correct: Agreement on named categories is close to the offline figure (89% vs 91%), so the model is not the main problem. The measurement was built from a labeled archive that excluded the unlabeled long tail, which is 38% of production volume. The success criterion must be re-derived from a representative live sample, and the large "other" share is itself a framing finding about the taxonomy and the human path.

distractors.B: Few-shot examples on the 14 categories target a weakness the evidence does not show, and re-passing the old offline eval would repeat the unrepresentative measurement.
distractors.C: The archive has almost no "other" examples, so reweighting cannot recreate that 38% segment; the reweighted figure would still be an estimate without the cases that matter.
distractors.D: Excluding 38% of volume hides the segment where the system behaves worst and still has to be handled by someone, so the bar would no longer reflect business outcomes.

scenario:
A claims-letter pipeline runs intake, extraction, drafting, mandatory human approval, and send. Letters approved without edit are promoted into the few-shot example pool on the assumption that they are good. Last quarter's review telemetry:
Letters approved without edit: 94%
Median reviewer time per letter (about 400 words): 11 seconds
Seeded-error audit (known defects injected into the queue): reviewers flagged 31%
Post-send complaints traced to drafting errors: up 3x since launch
stem: Which change to the feedback loop is most important?

options.text: Stop treating approval without edit as a quality signal; keep unaudited approvals out of the example pool, and build labels from seeded-error audits and double-reviewed samples.
Require reviewers to type a short justification for every approval, so each approved letter carries explicit reasoning that can be mined when choosing examples for the pool.
Have a second reviewer re-review each letter, and promote just the letters that both reviewers approve unchanged into the example pool as positive examples.
Raise reviewer staffing and set a one-minute minimum review time per letter, then continue promoting approved letters to the example pool as before.

rationale.correct: The evidence shows reviewers are not catching defects (31% seeded-error detection) even though 94% of letters pass unedited, so approval is not a label of quality. Feeding approvals back as positives amplifies the defects the loop was meant to remove. The feedback path needs labels with measured reliability, which seeded audits and double review provide.

distractors.B: Free-text justifications tend to become boilerplate under time pressure, and they do not measure whether the reviewer actually detected anything.
distractors.C: Dual review of every letter doubles review labor and time on the approval path, and two reviewers spending seconds each can still share the same blind spots, so the signal is not measured as reliable.
distractors.D: A time floor does not guarantee attention, nor measure detection, and the pool would still be fed by unaudited labels.

scenario: A nightly pipeline extracts invoice data with Claude, validates it, and posts approved invoices to an ERP that must be finished by 06:00. The ERP sometimes times out after it has already committed a posting, and retrying the whole job then creates duplicate postings. Model calls are the slow, costly stages. The ERP's create-invoice endpoint stores a client-supplied reference but does not enforce uniqueness, and it supports lookup by that reference.
stem: Select the TWO architecture changes that best stop duplicate postings without hurting the deadline or cost.

options.text: Record each invoice's state in the store, pending before the post and confirmed after, and on resume look up pending ones in the ERP by reference before deciding whether to post again.
Persist validated extractions, then run a separate commit stage that reads that store and posts to the ERP, so an ERP retry never re-runs a model call.
Retry the entire pipeline from the start after any ERP timeout with exponential backoff, since extraction is stable enough to reproduce the same results on a rerun.
Before each post, have Claude call an ERP search tool to check whether the invoice already exists and skip the post when it finds a match for the document.
Send a reference derived from the document ID with every ERP post and rely on the ERP to reject any repeat of that reference during a retry or a rerun.

rationale.correct: Duplicates arise from retrying a side-effecting step whose outcome is unknown. Persisting validated extractions and running a separate commit stage keeps retries out of the model calls, and recording pending and confirmed states with a lookup by reference lets a resumed commit stage learn whether a timed-out post committed. Together they make replay safe without re-running costly stages.

distractors.C: Rerunning from the start repeats the slow, costly model stages and still depends on the unsafe post being repeated; it threatens both deadline and cost.
distractors.D: A check-then-post sequence is racy, because a timed-out post may commit after the check, and delegating that check to a model adds non-determinism to a correctness control.
distractors.E: The ERP stores the reference but does not enforce uniqueness, so repeats are accepted and the duplicates still occur.

scenario: A retailer's customer-service assistant handles about 2M conversations a day in three categories: order questions (read-only order tools), returns (can issue prepaid labels and refunds up to $50), and account changes (can edit addresses and payment methods). The first response must arrive in under 3 seconds p95 and cost per conversation is tightly managed. In a prototype with one agent holding every tool, misrouted write actions were the main source of incidents.
stem: Which architecture best fits?

options.text: A routing workflow: a small model classifies each message into a structured enum that includes "unclear", then dispatches to a handler holding just that category's tools, with "unclear" going to a read-only clarifying handler.
A single agent with every tool and a system prompt rule that each write tool may only be used for its own category, plus server-side parameter checks and audit logging on each write tool.

A parallelization workflow in which all three handlers draft a reply at once and a selector call picks the best one, so routing mistakes are corrected by comparison before the reply is sent to the customer.
A routing workflow that uses the top-tier model as the router for maximum classification accuracy, dispatching to handlers that each hold only their own category's tools.

rationale.correct: The decisive constraints are least privilege for write tools and a tight latency and cost envelope at high volume. A cheap structured classification step followed by a handler holding only its own tools makes a misroute unable to perform another category's writes, and the "unclear" lane turns low-confidence routing into a safe read-only path. The extra hop is a small-model call, which fits the 3-second budget.

distractors.B: Parameter checks cannot tell whether a write is appropriate for the conversation, and the agent still holds every tool, so the incident class remains while every call carries the full tool definitions.
distractors.C: Three drafts roughly triple cost, and write-capable handlers could execute side effects before any selector chooses a winner.
distractors.D: The handler isolation is right, but a top-tier model on every one of 2M daily messages spends the cost and first-response latency budget on a classification that a small model with an "unclear" lane handles adequately.

scenario: A bank's marketing team generates product emails that must satisfy 40 regulatory phrasing rules. A deterministic linter already catches the 25 mechanical rules (required disclosures, banned phrases). The other 15 rules need judgment, such as "no implication of guaranteed approval". Generation runs as an overnight batch, so latency is secondary, but cost per approved email is tracked and compliance sign-off requires that unresolved emails reach a human. In a pilot, a cheaper evaluator tier agreed with compliance reviewers on 71% of the judgment-rule calls, against 93% for the strongest tier, and its false passes would reach customers.
stem: Select the TWO design elements that best make an evaluator-optimizer loop worthwhile here.

options.text: Run the linter first as a cheap gate and call the model evaluator only on drafts that pass it, scoring just the 15 judgment rules against a rubric with worked examples.
Have the generating call re-read its own draft against the full 40-rule list in the same conversation and revise until it states that no violations remain in the draft.
Cap revision rounds at two, feed the evaluator's per-rule findings rather than a rewritten draft back to the generator, and route emails still failing after the cap to compliance reviewers.
Use a cheaper model tier as the evaluator, since it only scores drafts against a fixed rubric, and keep the strongest tier for generation where quality matters.
Loop until the evaluator returns zero findings, since a hard iteration cap would let emails that still contain violations move forward in the approval workflow.

rationale.correct: An evaluator-optimizer loop pays off when the evaluator supplies an independent, checkable signal and the loop is bounded. Putting the deterministic linter first keeps the model evaluator on the 15 rules only it can judge, and bounded rounds with a human fallback satisfy both cost tracking and the sign-off requirement. Returning findings instead of a rewrite keeps the generator accountable for the fix.

distractors.B: Self-review in the same conversation shares the generator's blind spots and lets the model declare itself clean, so it gives no independent signal.
distractors.D: The pilot shows the cheaper tier agrees with compliance reviewers on only 71% of judgment-rule calls, so it would pass violating emails to customers, and the savings are outweighed by that risk.
distractors.E: An uncapped loop has unbounded cost, can oscillate, and an evaluator that never stops finding issues stalls the batch; the human route, not endless iteration, is the safeguard.

scenario: A health insurer's support assistant uses a coordinator with three subagents: billing, claims-status, and account-security. Only the account-security subagent needs a tool that reads full member identity records; the others need just the member ID and plan. Compliance requires data minimization and an audit of what each subagent accessed, and the team wants the subagents to run in parallel to keep p95 latency under 6 seconds.
stem: Select the THREE design choices that best satisfy both constraints.

options.text: Define each subagent with an explicit tool allowlist for its own domain, so the identity-record tool appears only in the account-security subagent's definition.
Have the coordinator give each subagent a scoped brief with the member ID, plan, and the specific question, rather than the full conversation transcript.
Require subagents to return structured results containing only the fields the coordinator needs plus a source reference, so identity details do not flow into the coordinator's context by default.
Have the coordinator look up the full member identity record once, up front, and pass it to all three subagents so none needs its own identity tool or repeats the lookup.
Populate a shared read-only member-context cache with the identity record for the session, so all three subagents read what they need without extra tool calls or added latency.

rationale.correct: Data minimization is enforced structurally at three points: which tools a subagent can call, what context it receives, and what flows back. Each is compatible with parallel execution because subagents stay independent and the coordinator only joins their compact results. These choices cut exposure without adding sequential waits.

distractors.D: A single coordinator-side lookup is efficient, but it puts full identity data in the coordinator and every subagent's context, which defeats minimization.
distractors.E: A shared cache saves calls, but it exposes the full record to subagents that do not need it and makes it harder to audit which subagent accessed which fields.

scenario: A refactoring coordinator splits a service migration across four worker subagents running in parallel in one shared checkout. In the last run, the integration suite failed after one worker's edit to a shared module silently overwrote another's, even though each worker's own unit tests passed. The delivery deadline rules out running the workers one after another. All four workers must touch the shared modules, so any wave schedule would collapse into sequential work.
stem: Which change best fixes this without giving up parallelism?

options.text: Have the coordinator assign disjoint file ownership and change shared modules first; give each worker its own git worktree branch, then merge in dependency order, running the integration suite after each merge.
Run the workers in two waves in the shared checkout, independent workers in parallel and dependent ones after them, ending each wave with an integration-suite run before the next wave begins.
Have each worker take an advisory lock file before editing any shared file and release it once its own tests pass, so two workers do not edit one file at the same time during the run.
Give each worker its own git worktree branch with no up-front ownership split, and resolve any conflicts when the coordinator merges the four branches together at the end of the run.

rationale.correct: The failure is concurrent writes to shared state, which workers' own unit tests cannot detect. Disjoint ownership plus isolated worktrees removes the contention while preserving parallel work, and merging in dependency order with an integration run per merge is where cross-worker defects are caught. Handling shared modules first by the coordinator removes the main source of overlap.

distractors.B: Waves reduce, but do not remove, overwrites inside a wave in a shared checkout, and the second wave adds wall-clock time the deadline cannot absorb.
distractors.C: Advisory locks held until tests pass serialize work on hot files anyway, depend on agents honoring them, and leave stale locks when a worker fails.
distractors.D: Worktrees isolate edits, but without ownership two workers still change the same shared module, and the conflicts then surface at the end of the run in one large merge.

scenario: A law firm's eDiscovery team must review 1.2 million emails for responsiveness within three weeks. Missing a responsive document carries sanction risk, so the agreed protocol requires at least 98% recall; false positives only cost reviewer time. Running the top-tier model on every email would exceed the budget about sixfold. In a prior matter, opposing counsel's expert had a production's recall claim thrown out because it was a point estimate computed on the same sample used to set the threshold.
stem: Which decomposition best fits?

options.text: A two-stage funnel: tune the small model's threshold on one labeled sample, require the lower confidence bound on held-out recall to clear 98% with margin for stage two, let a stronger model review survivors, and audit sampled rejects.

A two-stage funnel: tune the small model's threshold on one labeled sample, confirm on a separate held-out sample that measured recall is at least 98%, and have a stronger model review the survivors to produce the final labels for the review set.

A two-stage funnel: a small model scores each email with its threshold chosen to maximize F1 on a labeled validation sample, and a stronger model reviews the survivors to produce the final labels for production.
Pre-filter with the firm's existing keyword search terms, and have the strongest model review every keyword hit, which reduces the volume enough to fit the budget for the three-week review window.

rationale.correct: The prior challenge names two defects: a point estimate, and evaluation on the tuning sample. Option A fixes both — a held-out sample removes the tuning bias, and a lower confidence bound (not the point estimate) is what must clear 98%. It also leaves margin for responsive emails the stage-two model wrongly drops, since end-to-end recall is the product of both stages, and the reject audit gives defensible evidence about what the funnel discarded. The funnel itself is what makes the budget work: the cheap model screens all 1.2 million emails and the strong model sees only survivors.

distractors.B: B fixes only half of the prior challenge: a held-out sample removes tuning bias, but a measured recall of exactly 98% is still a point estimate whose true value could be well below 98%. It also treats stage-one recall as the system's recall, ignoring responsive emails the stronger model later rejects, and provides no evidence about discarded emails.
distractors.C: Maximizing F1 treats false positives and false negatives alike, so the threshold would discard responsive emails to save second-stage cost and miss the recall requirement.
distractors.D: Keyword filters are blind to paraphrase and code words, so recall is uncontrolled and unmeasured, which the protocol does not accept.

scenario: A monthly job checks 200 annual reports of about 300 pages each for internal consistency: the same figures (revenue, headcount, emissions) and commitments are restated in different sections and must agree. A one-pass whole-report call is too costly at this volume, and an earlier attempt that summarized sections first lost exact figures. Every finding must cite both locations.
stem: Select the TWO decomposition elements that best fit.

options.text: Process sections in parallel, each extracting every figure and commitment into a schema with entity, period, value, unit, and page, so no section call needs another section's context.
Compare the extracted entries in code by entity, period, and unit, and send only conflicting pairs, with their surrounding excerpts, to Claude to judge whether each conflict is real or definitional.
Summarize each section, then summarize the summaries hierarchically into a report-level digest, and ask Claude to flag contradictions found in the digest across the report.
Build an embedding index over all section text, retrieve the nearest restatements of each figure across sections, and have Claude compare the retrieved passages for agreement.
Choose the two sections most likely to restate each other by keyword overlap on shared figures, and give a single call both sections in full, repeating for each section pair.

rationale.correct: The cross-cutting requirement is matching exact values across distant sections. Extracting to a schema in parallel turns the problem into structured data, and a deterministic comparison in code finds candidate conflicts cheaply, reserving model judgment for the few pairs where semantics matter. Both locations are preserved as fields, satisfying the citation requirement.

distractors.C: Hierarchical summaries drop exact figures, the same flaw that sank the earlier attempt.
distractors.D: Semantic similarity retrieves text about the same topic but not reliably the same entity, period, and unit, so mismatches are missed, and the check depends on retrieval quality rather than exact comparison.
distractors.E: Keyword-based pairing misses restatements that use different wording, and the number of pair calls grows quickly with sections per report.

scenario:
Eight weeks after launching a Claude first-response assistant, the VP reports cost per resolved ticket fell from $6.05 to $4.47 (26%) and wants that figure in the board ROI case. A marketing campaign began the same week and shifted ticket mix toward easy categories. A holdout group is not permitted because every customer must get the same service. Cost per resolved ticket and share of volume, before launch then now:
Password/login: $1.80 then $1.60; 20% then 45%
Billing disputes: $6.40 then $6.10; 35% then 25%
Technical faults: $8.00 then $7.60; 30% then 18%
Account closure/legal: $7.00 then $7.10; 15% then 12%
stem: What should the ROI case report?

options.text: Re-weight the current per-category costs to the pre-launch mix (about $5.80 against $6.05), report that change with per-category figures, and note that without a holdout it shows association, not proven cause.

Report the 26% blended reduction with a footnote that traffic mix changed, since blended cost per resolved ticket is the figure the company actually pays now, and the easiest one for the board to audit.
Report per-category costs before and after with no blended figure, noting that three of four categories improved, and let the board judge the impact from the table.
Report cost per resolved ticket for human-handled tickets alone, since that isolates the labor the assistant removed from the support queue.

rationale.correct: Most of the headline drop comes from the volume shifting to the cheapest category, not from the assistant. Holding the mix fixed at the pre-launch weights isolates the cost change due to the solution, and the evidence shows it is about 4%, with account closure getting slightly worse. With no holdout, standardizing for mix is the defensible way to attribute the change.

distractors.B: A footnote does not fix the headline; the board would read a 26% improvement that the evidence attributes mostly to the campaign's mix.
distractors.C: The table is honest, but it gives the board no volume-weighted ROI figure, and without a standardized total each reader will mentally re-weight to the current mix and overstate the saving.
distractors.D: Human-handled tickets are now a harder subset because the assistant resolves the easy ones, so their cost is not comparable with the pre-launch population.

scenario: A business-process outsourcer sells document processing at a fixed fee per accepted claim and plans to quadruple volume with a Claude pipeline. Average model cost per claim looks acceptable today, but token use varies widely with document length: the longest 10% of claims consume about 45% of tokens. A smaller model's lower unit price brings noticeably more rework on complex claims. The contract allows adding a surcharge tier for oversized claims with 60 days' notice.
stem: Which measurement-and-control approach best aligns the design with the cost pillar?

options.text: Track fully loaded cost per accepted claim (model, review, and rework) by document-length decile, set a per-claim token budget, and route claims beyond it to the surcharge tier or a human-assisted path.
Track average model cost per claim and negotiate volume pricing at the new scale, since the average is what the fixed fee must cover across the quadrupled claim volume and any added capacity.
Track fully loaded cost per accepted claim by length decile, and move the longest-document tail to the smallest tier, since that tail drives 45% of token spend.
Track reviewer minutes per claim and drive them down by auto-accepting any claim whose model confidence is above a fixed threshold across all document lengths.

rationale.correct: Margin under a fixed per-claim fee is set by the fully loaded cost per accepted claim, and the long tail dominates it. Looking at deciles exposes where margin is lost, and a token budget with a surcharge or human path uses the contract's lever. Averages and unit-price cuts hide the tail and shift cost into rework.

distractors.B: The average hides that the longest claims consume nearly half of tokens; volume pricing does not change that distribution.
distractors.C: The measurement is right, but the longest documents are the complex ones where the smaller tier raises rework, so shifting them can lift fully loaded cost per accepted claim.
distractors.D: Confidence-based auto-accept optimizes review time only, can pass more errors that return as rework, and ignores token cost on long documents.

scenario: An organization delivers managed policy two ways: server-managed settings from the claude.ai admin console, and a managed-settings.json pushed by configuration management. The file goes to contractor laptops (signed in with the organization account, not MDM-enrolled) and to Linux dev servers and CI runners that use Amazon Bedrock and never receive console policy. The file holds the secrets deny rules; the console policy holds only model and plugin settings. Team leads can write to the file's directory on every machine and keep local allow rules and hooks there. A security review finds Claude can read `.env` files on the laptops but is denied on the servers.
stem: What is the root cause, and which fix best fits these constraints?

options.text: Two managed paths do not compose by default, so the console policy hides the file on laptops; generate both the console policy and the file from one source-controlled rule set so each path is a complete policy.

Set `managedSourcesBehavior` to "merge" so each delivery path contributes, which makes the laptops apply the file's deny rules alongside the console policy's model and plugin settings and keeps one copy of the rules.

Retire the console policy and deliver the whole policy through MDM, so a single managed source applies on each machine and the secrets deny rules are selected wherever Claude Code runs in the organization.

Commit the deny rules to each repository's `.claude/settings.json`, since deny rules apply immediately without a trust step, and leave the managed file in place for the Linux servers and the CI runners.

rationale.correct: By default Claude Code takes the policy from the highest-ranked managed source that sets a policy key. On the laptops the console policy outranks the file, so the file's deny rules are skipped, while the servers never get console policy and so use the file. Generating both from one rule set makes each path a complete policy, so whichever source is selected enforces the deny rules.

distractors.B: Merge would apply the file's deny rules on the laptops, but it also adds the file's lists, including the allow rules and hooks team leads write there, to enforced policy; it is meant for cases where every lower source is admin-controlled, and here it is not.
distractors.C: Retiring the console policy requires enrolling the contractor laptops in MDM, which the scenario rules out, and the laptops would then depend on a channel they cannot receive.
distractors.D: Repository-level deny rules reach only repositories that carry the file and can be edited in a clone, so they do not provide fleet-wide enforcement.

scenario: A platform team is standardizing Claude Code across 40 repositories. Requirements: (1) secrets paths such as `.env*` and `~/.aws/**` must never be readable, in any repository, including those with no Claude configuration; (2) each team's repo-specific allow rules and plugin marketplace should reach teammates through version control on first clone, and teams should be able to adjust them; (3) the platform team does not want to review every team's rule changes.
stem: Select the TWO placements that best satisfy these requirements.

options.text: Put the secrets deny rules in managed settings, delivered by MDM or a managed file, where no user, project, or command-line value can override them.

Put each team's allow rules and marketplace declaration in its repository's committed `.claude/settings.json`, so teammates receive them in interactive sessions through version control once they trust the folder.
Put the secrets deny rules in each repository's committed `.claude/settings.json`, because deny rules apply immediately without a trust step and travel with the code.
Put each team's allow rules in managed settings with `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, so the rules are identical and tamper-resistant across the 40 repositories.
Put each team's allow rules in `.claude/settings.local.json` and distribute that file from a shared template repository so it matches across each clone of the repository.

rationale.correct: Requirement 1 spans every repository and must resist override, which is what the managed tier provides. Requirements 2 and 3 describe team-owned configuration, which belongs in the committed project file; its allow rules and marketplace take effect after the folder is trusted, the intended gate. Splitting the placements by who owns each rule satisfies all three.

distractors.C: Committed deny rules protect only repositories that carry the file and can be edited in a clone, so repos without Claude configuration remain exposed.
distractors.D: Restricting permissions to managed rules removes teams' own allow rules and makes the platform team the bottleneck for every change, violating requirement 3.
distractors.E: The local file is personal and normally untracked, so it is not a sharing mechanism, and a tracked local file still goes through the trust step.

scenario:
A CI job runs Claude Code headless on each PR to cross-check the diff against the linked ticket, using a ticketing MCP server supplied by a config file in the pipeline repository. Last week three PRs passed review even though their tickets required changes the diff lacked.
mcp-ci.json: {"mcpServers": {"ticketing": {"url": "https://tickets.internal.example/mcp"}}}
Step: claude -p "$PROMPT" --mcp-config mcp-ci.json --output-format stream-json --verbose (stderr captured by the runner)
Step exit code: 0
Final result text: "No ticket details were available, so I checked the diff for general quality only. LGTM."
stem: What is the root cause and the best fix?

options.text: The `url` entry lacks a `type`, so validation skipped the server and the run exited 0; add it, and fail CI when the init event shows a non-empty `mcp_server_errors` or no `ticketing` server.
Add the missing `type` to the entry, and fail CI unless the stream contains a tool call to a `ticketing` tool, so any review that never consulted the ticket is rejected.
The MCP server timed out at startup; raise the `MCP_TIMEOUT` value and add a retry on non-zero exit, so a slow server cannot silently degrade the review on a busy shared runner.
Claude ignored the missing tool; tighten the prompt so it must answer "UNABLE TO REVIEW" whenever a ticket cannot be fetched, and fail the step when that string appears in the output.

rationale.correct: The review text and exit code show the tool never existed in the session, not that it failed at run time. Entries that fail validation, such as a `url` entry with no `type`, are skipped and the run continues and exits cleanly, with the details reported only in the init event's `mcp_server_errors` when stderr is captured. A gate on that field converts a silent degradation into a failed check.

distractors.B: Gating on a tool call relies on model behavior: a PR that legitimately needs no lookup would fail, and a still-broken config is detected only after a full review has run, when the init event reports the cause directly.
distractors.C: A startup timeout would not produce a clean exit with the server absent, and the exit code is 0, so a retry on non-zero exit would never fire.
distractors.D: Those flags control which other MCP sources load, not whether this entry validates, so the server would still be skipped.

scenario: A platform team runs a nightly `claude -p` repo-health job across 300 repositories on a shared runner pool. Last Tuesday one repository's run looped on a flaky test and used about 40x the median spend before the 3-hour job timeout. Finance wants each run's spend bounded and attributable, a single runaway must not stop the other 299 repositories, and cost per repository should be visible without waiting for the monthly invoice.
stem: Select the TWO changes that best meet these requirements.

options.text: Set `--max-budget-usd` on each run below the highest cost tolerable for one repository, leaving headroom because spend can pass the cap, and bound turns with `--max-turns`.
Use `--output-format json` and record each run's `total_cost_usd`, turns, and repository in the metrics store, treating the figure as an estimate for alerting rather than billing.
Split the repositories across ten workspaces, each with its own API key and a monthly spend limit sized to its share, so overruns stay contained to a group and spend is attributable per group.
Give each of the 300 runs a 20-minute wall-clock timeout instead of the 3-hour job timeout, so a looping run is cut off long before it can reach 40x the median spend.
Run each job with `--permission-mode dontAsk` and a narrow `--allowedTools` list that excludes the test runner, so an agent cannot loop on a flaky test.

rationale.correct: A per-run cap contains a runaway where it happens, and because the client-side check can overshoot, the cap must sit below the tolerable ceiling rather than at it. Recording the JSON result's cost per repository gives attribution and timely alerting, with the caveat that it is an estimate. Other repositories keep running because limits are per run.

distractors.C: A runaway still exhausts its workspace's limit and stops about thirty healthy repositories for the rest of the month, and attribution is only per group rather than per run.
distractors.D: Wall-clock time is a proxy for spend: a fast, token-heavy run can still cost far above the median in 20 minutes, and the timeout gives no per-repository cost record.
distractors.E: Restricting tools removes one loop trigger, but a run can loop on reads, edits, or reasoning, so spend stays unbounded and nothing is attributed.

scenario:
A support product and a nightly summarization backfill share one API key and workspace. At 02:10 the backfill started 200 concurrent workers; interactive chat p95 rose from 2.1 s to 19 s and some chats failed. Each backfill item is a multi-step tool-use loop, due by 08:00 and not user-facing. Excerpts:
02:09 backfill start workers=200
02:10 rate_limit_error (429) share: interactive 8%, backfill 31%
02:10 429 responses carry a retry-after header; SDK max_retries=2 on both clients
Interactive request rate unchanged at about 40 per second
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Cap backfill concurrency with a client-side limiter that leaves headroom for interactive traffic, and add jittered backoff to its retries.
Raise `max_retries` on both clients so that rate-limited requests retry more times before surfacing an error to the chat user or to the backfill job that is running overnight.
Move the backfill to the Message Batches API, since the work is asynchronous and not user-facing, so it no longer competes with interactive traffic for the shared limit.
Give the backfill its own API key in the same workspace, so its traffic is separately attributable and can be revoked or throttled independently if it misbehaves again.

rationale.correct: Interactive volume is unchanged, so the contention comes from the backfill's burst against a shared limit. Bounding backfill concurrency and honoring retry-after protects the interactive path while letting the backfill finish before 08:00. This is a control at the source of the load rather than more retries.

distractors.B: More retries from 200 workers add load during the very window of rejection, deepening the congestion and raising interactive latency further.
distractors.C: Batching suits single-request items, but each backfill item is a multi-step tool-use loop that cannot be expressed as one batched request.
distractors.D: A separate key identifies and can revoke the backfill's traffic, but it does not allocate capacity: both keys still draw on the same rate limits, so the burst would again starve interactive requests.

scenario: A claims assistant built on Claude tool use shows intermittent malformed tool calls for one tenant, a hospital network, in about 4% of sessions; other tenants are under 0.2%. The hospital's contract limits retention of prompts and tool outputs to 24 hours and pins the model snapshot it validated; any new logging of tool outputs needs a change request with a two-week lead time. Request IDs, model and prompt versions, token counts, stop reasons, tool names, and argument-validity flags are logged for all tenants indefinitely. The hospital also validated one earlier snapshot, and runs about 150 sessions a day.
stem: Select the THREE actions that best localize the cause within these constraints.

options.text: Compare logged metadata for the hospital's failing and succeeding sessions against other tenants: stop reasons, input token counts, tool names, and validation-failure types.
Replay captured failing requests from the 24-hour window in staging, redacted as the contract permits, against the pinned model and prompt versions, changing one factor at a time.
Inspect the hospital's tool definitions and tenant-specific tool results, such as unusually long or oddly encoded fields, for features that could disrupt argument generation.
Canary the hospital tenant on the earlier snapshot it has already validated for 24 hours, and compare its malformed-call rate with the current snapshot's rate for that tenant.
Enable sampled full-content capture for just the hospital tenant, retained for 24 hours, to see the exact arguments in failing calls as they occur in production traffic.

rationale.correct: The failures are tenant-specific, so the investigation should find what differs about this tenant using data that is already retained, and then test hypotheses on replays inside the retention window. Comparing metadata, replaying controlled variants, and inspecting tenant-specific tool surface area do this without touching healthy tenants or breaching retention limits.

distractors.D: At about 150 sessions a day and a 4% rate, 24 hours yields roughly six failures, too few to separate a snapshot effect from noise, and it still needs the hospital's sign-off to switch snapshots; controlled replays give a cleaner comparison.
distractors.E: New logging of tool outputs for this tenant needs a change request with a two-week lead time, so it cannot be turned on now, and replaying existing failing requests inside the retention window gives the same evidence.

scenario:
A team moved a tagging route to the next model generation by changing only the model ID. The route was validated at a 0.9 s p95 with thinking off. A client wrapper retries on a 400 by stripping the rejected parameters. The team must stay on the new generation. Logs and metrics:
attempt 1: 400 invalid_request_error (thinking, temperature)
attempt 2: parameters stripped, 200 OK
p95 latency: 0.9 s before, 3.4 s after
average output tokens: 60 before, 410 after
accuracy: 94.1% before, 94.3% after
stem: Select the THREE actions that best address the cause.

options.text: Make the wrapper fail loudly on rejected parameters, and run a staging check against the new model before any model ID change.
Re-run an effort sweep on this route, including whatever thinking control the new model documents, and pick the lowest effort that holds accuracy.
After the sweep, record the chosen effort and thinking setting in the route's config, and reset the baselines and alerts to the new model.
Keep the stripping wrapper and raise the client timeout so the slower calls stop failing downstream.
Move the route to a smaller tier at the default setting, since a smaller model should answer faster without a sweep.

rationale.correct: The evidence shows the old request settings were silently dropped, so the route fell back to the new model's default thinking and effort: output tokens rose almost sevenfold and p95 latency nearly quadrupled with no accuracy gain. The durable fixes are to stop silent parameter stripping, re-baseline the route by sweeping effort for the new model, and reset the baselines so later drift is measured against the new model.

distractors.D: A longer timeout hides the latency regression and keeps the silent stripping that caused it, so the next model change will fail the same way.
distractors.E: Without a sweep the smaller model also runs at its default thinking and effort, so the cause persists and quality on the route is unvalidated.

scenario: A support assistant runs a cascade: Haiku 5.5 answers first, and tickets it marks low confidence escalate to Opus 5.5. With the cached 40,000-token prefix, one attempt costs about 1 unit on Haiku, 10 units on Sonnet 5.5, and 20 units on Opus. The forecast assumed 12% escalation; the observed rate is 30%, so cost per ticket is above forecast. Hard tickets cannot be predicted from ticket text or metadata, and quality on them must match Opus.
stem: What should the team do about the overrun?

options.text: Rebuild the forecast on the observed 30% escalation and keep the cascade, at about 7 units against 10 for mid-tier.
Replace the cascade with Sonnet 5.5 on all traffic, which removes both the failed first attempt and the escalation step.
Tighten the Haiku confidence threshold so fewer tickets escalate to Opus, and accept the extra reopened tickets that follow.
Add a content-based classifier that sends likely-hard tickets straight to Opus 5.5 and skips the Haiku attempt.

rationale.correct: Cascade cost per ticket is 1 + 0.3 x 20 = 7 units, against 10 for a mid-tier model on everything, so the cascade is still the cheaper design and the forecast was what was wrong. The right response is to correct the forecast with measured rates, not to redesign.

distractors.B: Mid-tier on all traffic costs 10 units per ticket, which is more than the cascade's 7 even after the failed Haiku attempts are counted.
distractors.C: A tighter threshold sends fewer hard tickets to Opus, so wrong Haiku answers reach customers and quality on hard tickets drops below the Opus level required.
distractors.D: Hardness is not predictable from ticket text, so the classifier misroutes and itself costs a call, adding spend without reliably skipping Haiku.

scenario: A banking assistant on Sonnet 5.5 runs long sessions behind a cached 25,000-token system prompt. When the fraud engine flags an account mid-session, the assistant must switch to a restricted mode that withholds balances. Today the backend rewrites the top-level system prompt for the rest of the session, and the next request after each flag shows a full cache write. Security also wants the switch instruction to carry operator authority that a customer message cannot imitate.
stem: Which change best meets both needs?

options.text: Append a system-role message with the restricted-mode instruction after the latest user turn and leave the cached prefix unchanged.
Add the restricted-mode text to the next user message inside an operator tag that the system prompt already declares trustworthy.
Keep a second cached system prompt that already contains restricted mode, and switch the request to it when the flag arrives.
End the session and open a new conversation whose system prompt includes the restricted mode plus a summary of earlier turns.

rationale.correct: A mid-conversation system message is appended to messages instead of editing top-level system, so the cached prefix stays intact, and it travels in the operator channel customers cannot write to. Its placement rule (after a user turn, last or followed by an assistant turn) is easy to meet at a mid-session flag.

distractors.B: Text in a user message arrives in the customer-writable channel, so a customer can imitate the tag and the authority requirement fails.
distractors.C: A second system prompt is a different prefix, so the switch rewrites the whole prefix and history exactly as today, and two prompts must be kept in step.
distractors.D: A new conversation also writes a fresh cache entry and discards session state, adding summarization loss without meeting the cache goal.

scenario: After a prompt refresh on Opus 5.5, an order-support assistant skips the order-lookup tool on 34% of order questions and answers from memory. The refresh added the line: 'CRITICAL: NEVER call a tool unless you are ABSOLUTELY certain it is required. Unnecessary calls are UNACCEPTABLE.' Tool calls per ticket fell 40%, which was the goal, but accuracy on order-status questions fell from 96% to 81%. Cost still has to come down. Answers stream straight to the customer under a 3-second budget.
stem: Select the TWO changes, one fix and one guard, that best address the regression while keeping the cost goal.

options.text: Replace the emphatic rule with a plain statement of when a lookup is needed (any order-specific claim) and why, noting that general policy questions need none.
Add paired eval cases that fail on both missed lookups and needless lookups, and gate prompt changes on them.
Add few-shot examples that show a lookup on order questions and none on policy questions, and leave the emphatic rule in place.
Raise effort to max so the model reasons longer about whether a lookup is required before skipping one.
Add a code validator that rejects order answers lacking a lookup result and re-prompts the model to call the tool.

rationale.correct: Emphatic prohibitions are over-weighted by recent models, which then under-trigger the tool; a scoped rule with its reason restores lookups where they matter and keeps them off for policy questions, preserving the savings. The regression slipped through because no eval measured the opposite failure, so a two-direction eval is the guard.

distractors.C: Examples sit beside a rule that still tells the model to avoid tools, adding cached tokens while the conflicting instruction remains, so the 34% skip rate is unlikely to close.
distractors.D: More reasoning does not correct a rule that tells the model to avoid the tool, and the extra tokens work against the cost goal.
distractors.E: A re-prompt after a skipped lookup is a second model call, which does not fit a 3-second streamed budget, and the answer has already begun streaming to the customer.

scenario: An insurer's claims-triage route on Opus 5.5 must return a JSON decision within a 6-second p95, and auditors want a short human-readable justification stored with each decision. The current prompt says 'think step by step inside <analysis> tags, then output JSON.' About 2% of responses fail parsing when the analysis text contains braces, and median output has grown to 1,800 tokens, most of it analysis.
stem: Which redesign best meets the latency, parsing, and audit needs?

options.text: Drop the step-by-step instruction, let built-in thinking do the reasoning, and use structured outputs with a short justification field.
Keep the <analysis> block but move it after the JSON so the decision streams to the caller first and the justification follows it.
Keep the visible step-by-step analysis and tighten the extraction parser so that brace characters inside the analysis text no longer break it.
Turn thinking off for the route and ask for a chain of thought of two numbered sentences before the JSON, bounding the length of the output.

rationale.correct: The model already reasons internally, so a visible chain of thought duplicates that work and inflates output tokens. Structured outputs remove the brace-parsing failure at the source, and a short justification field satisfies the auditors without a long free-text analysis. Effort is then the latency lever.

distractors.B: Reordering saves time-to-decision but keeps free text beside the JSON, so the parsing fault remains and the long analysis still generates.
distractors.C: A stricter parser patches the symptom and leaves the 1,800-token output, which is the latency problem.
distractors.D: Two sentences of free text before the JSON keep the unstructured-output parsing fault, and removing built-in thinking lowers decision quality to save a few tokens.

scenario:
A fraud-review prompt uses eight few-shot examples and is cached across 40,000 requests a day. A calibration run compares labels:
few-shot example labels: 7 approve, 1 escalate
human labels on 400 held-out cases: 70% approve, 30% escalate
model labels on the same cases: 91% approve, 9% escalate
of the 120 true escalations, the model catches 32 (27% recall)
An earlier trial that added an 'escalate when uncertain' sentence, with the examples unchanged, moved the model's escalate rate only from 9% to 11%.
stem: Select the TWO changes most likely to fix the under-escalation.

options.text: Rebalance the examples so escalate cases make up roughly a third of the set instead of one in eight.
Pair near-identical cases that differ in one deciding factor, so the examples teach the boundary rather than surface features.
Reshuffle the example order on every request so that no label holds a favored position.
Add eight more examples drawn at random from the live queue, since a larger sample reduces skew.
Strengthen the 'escalate when uncertain' sentence and drop the examples that conflict with it.

rationale.correct: The examples are 87.5% approve against a true 70%, and the model's 91% approve rate shows it following that prior; recall is 27%. Rebalancing fixes the prior the examples teach, and contrast pairs teach what actually decides an escalation. The instruction alone has already been tried and barely moved the rate.

distractors.C: Reshuffling per request changes the prefix every time and defeats caching on a 40,000-request route, without correcting the label skew.
distractors.D: Random draws from the live queue reproduce a mostly-approve mix and do not target the boundary, so the skew and the weak boundary learning largely persist.
distractors.E: The instruction was tried and moved escalation from 9% to 11%, so strengthening it is unlikely to close a gap to 30%, and dropping examples removes the boundary cases.

scenario: A code-migration agent on Opus 5.5 runs sessions of about 300 turns. Each turn adds a tool result of 3,000 to 8,000 tokens, and the model must quote exact line numbers from results up to about 20 turns old. Prompt caching is on and sessions run continuously. Late in sessions, context passes 600K tokens and both latency and cost climb.
stem: Which context-management setup fits best?

options.text: Clear old tool results with context editing, using a high trigger and a large minimum clear, and keep the last 30 turns.
Clear the oldest tool result on every turn, so context holds a rolling window of only the most recent tool results.
Enable server-side compaction at its default threshold, so earlier turns are summarized into a compaction block as context grows.
Truncate each tool result to its first 1,500 tokens as it arrives, before it ever enters the conversation history.

rationale.correct: Clearing edits the prefix, so every clear forces a cache rewrite from the edit point onward. Clearing rarely and in large batches keeps rewrites infrequent, and retaining the last 30 turns keeps a margin over the 20 turns of exact results the model must quote.

distractors.B: Clearing every turn changes the prefix on every request, so the cache is rewritten constantly and latency and cost rise rather than fall.
distractors.C: A summary does not reliably preserve exact line numbers from recent results, and compaction also rewrites the cached history.
distractors.D: Truncating on arrival discards data that may sit past 1,500 tokens and was needed later, so exactness is lost.

scenario: An IT-operations agent on Sonnet 5.5 exposes 74 tools from five MCP servers. Each request carries about 31,000 tokens of tool definitions, 2,600 tokens of system prompt, and roughly 4,800 tokens of conversation history. Tool-selection accuracy is 83%, down from 94% when the agent had 20 tools. Sessions often touch three or four servers, most use fewer than six distinct tools, and the prefix is cached and shared across users.
stem: Select the TWO changes that best restore selection accuracy and cut prefill without losing cache reuse.

options.text: Mark rarely used tools as deferred and let tool search load them on demand, keeping a few core tools loaded.
Merge overlapping tools and rewrite descriptions so each tool's purpose is distinct and the definitions shrink.
Run a small classifier on each request to pick the 15 most relevant tools and send only those.
Compact the conversation history more aggressively, since history is the main driver of the excess tokens.
Split the agent into one agent per server with its own tool list and put a router in front of them.

rationale.correct: The definitions dominate the prefix and the model is choosing among too many overlapping options. Deferred loading keeps the cached prefix small and stable while rare tools are discovered when needed, and consolidating overlapping tools reduces both tokens and ambiguity. Neither changes the shared prefix per request.

distractors.C: A per-request tool subset changes the tools block, which sits at the start of the prefix, so each distinct subset invalidates the cache.
distractors.D: History is about 4,800 tokens against 31,000 for tool definitions, so compacting it addresses a minor share of the problem.
distractors.E: Sessions often span three or four servers, so the router adds hops and cross-agent handoffs while each agent still carries a large list.

scenario:
An order-support service on Opus 5.5 runs on four pods with three worker processes each. Every worker builds its tool list from an unordered collection at startup, producing about 12 distinct orderings. Traffic is about one request per 90 seconds overall, the shared prefix (tools plus system prompt) is 9,800 tokens, and a breakpoint sits on the system block. The measured cache hit rate is 24%. Sampled usage:
worker a tools=[search_docs,get_order,refund] cache_creation=9840 cache_read=0
worker b tools=[get_order,refund,search_docs] cache_creation=9840 cache_read=0
worker c tools=[refund,search_docs,get_order] cache_creation=0 cache_read=9840
worker d tools=[get_order,search_docs,refund] cache_creation=9840 cache_read=0
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Serialize the tool list in one canonical order, such as sorted by name, in every worker.
Switch the breakpoint to a one-hour lifetime so that each worker's ordering stays cached between its requests.
Pin each client to one pod with sticky routing so that every session sees only a few orderings.
Defer the tools through tool search so the tool list leaves the cached prefix altogether.

rationale.correct: The tools block sits at the start of the prefix, so each of the 12 orderings is a separate cache entry. At one request per 90 seconds, each ordering recurs about every 18 minutes, so a five-minute entry is reused roughly a quarter of the time, matching the 24% measured. One canonical order makes every worker share one entry that is re-read about every 90 seconds, about 96% of requests.

distractors.B: A one-hour lifetime would raise hits, but it keeps 12 entries alive and pays the 2x write premium on each every hour, about 27 units per hour against about 5 for one canonical entry.
distractors.C: Sticky routing leaves several orderings per pod, so each entry still sees a small share of traffic and load skews across pods.
distractors.D: Deferring tools is a larger redesign that changes tool selection behavior to cure a problem a stable ordering already solves.

scenario: A platform serves 400 tenants from one Opus 5.5 route. Each prompt has a 12,000-token shared policy section and a 2,000-token tenant section (brand voice, glossary). The tenant section currently comes first. The platform as a whole sends several requests per second, but any one tenant sends a request only every 10 to 20 minutes. Costs are high and cache reads are rare. Take a cache write as 1.25x base price (5-minute lifetime) or 2x (one hour), and a read as 0.1x.
stem: Select the TWO changes that best raise cache reads and lower cost.

options.text: Put the shared policy first with the only breakpoint after it, so every tenant reads the same cached prefix.
Keep the shared text byte-identical across tenants, with names, dates, and similar values only in the tenant section.
Keep the tenant section first with its own breakpoint, so that each tenant's prefix is cached separately from every other tenant's.
Keep the tenant section first and cache the whole 14,000-token prompt for each tenant with a one-hour lifetime.
Add a second breakpoint after the tenant section, so that each tenant's complete prompt is also cached for later requests.

rationale.correct: Caching matches on prefix, so the shared 12,000 tokens must come first and stay byte-identical for every tenant; then with several platform-wide requests per second that entry is always warm at about 0.1x per read. The 2,000-token tenant tail then costs full price, which beats paying a write premium on entries that expire before the tenant's next request.

distractors.C: A tenant-first prefix makes every entry tenant-specific, and the 10 to 20 minute gaps outlast the default lifetime, so reads stay rare.
distractors.D: Per tenant per hour this costs about 2x for one write plus three reads at 0.1x, near 2.3 units of 14,000 tokens over four requests, or roughly 8,000 token-equivalents per request, against about 3,200 when the shared prefix is read and the tenant tail pays full price.
distractors.E: With gaps of 10 to 20 minutes the default-lifetime tenant entry has expired before the next request, so the write premium of 1.25x is paid and never read.

scenario:
A team chooses between Sonnet 5.5 (model A) and Haiku 5.5 (model B) for an agent that reads untrusted web pages. The security team set a 95% injection block target and will approve the cheaper model only with evidence that it meets the target and with accuracy loss under 3 points. The launch date is fixed, the attack suite cannot be extended before it, and traffic cannot be split by risk level before launch. Eval readout:
model A: accuracy 91.2%, injections blocked 246/250 (98.4%), $4.10 per 1k tasks
model B: accuracy 89.8%, injections blocked 233/250 (93.2%), $0.70 per 1k tasks
model B block rate, 95% interval: about 90.1% to 96.3%
A screening layer for page content would add about $0.40 per 1k tasks and has not been run against the suite.
stem: What should the team do for this launch?

options.text: Ship model A now and revisit model B after the injection suite grows, accepting the higher cost per task.
Ship model B with the screening layer added, since the layer should lift its block rate above the target.
Ship model B and watch injection attempts closely, since its interval still reaches the 95% target.
Combine accuracy, cost, and block rate into one weighted score and pick whichever model has the higher total score.

rationale.correct: Evidence of meeting the target means more than an interval that touches it, and B's lower bound is about 90.1%, so B is not approved on this data. Only A has demonstrated the target. The screening layer is untested against the suite, which cannot be extended before launch, so it cannot supply the missing evidence, and traffic cannot be split to limit exposure.

distractors.B: The layer's effect on block rate is a hypothesis; with no run against the suite there is still no evidence, and it also reduces B's cost advantage.
distractors.C: An interval that merely reaches the target does not show the target is met, and close monitoring detects incidents after the fact rather than providing the evidence required.
distractors.D: A weighted score lets a large cost advantage buy back a safety shortfall, which a security target exists to prevent.

scenario: A security team will track prompt-injection resilience for an email agent on Sonnet 5.5 that can send messages and update calendars. Each release is run against a frozen suite of attack cases spanning 12 attack categories, plus a benign-task suite, and the release decision should rest on a small set of metrics.
stem: Select the THREE metrics that together best support a release decision.

options.text: Unauthorized-action rate: the share of attack cases in which a send or update tool call actually executes, measured at the tool layer.
Worst-category attack success rate, reported next to the pooled rate so a weak category cannot hide.
Benign-task success with defenses on versus off, so a defense that blocks legitimate work shows up.
Pooled attack success rate across all 12 categories with a 95% interval, reported as the release headline.
Time to detect and block live injection attempts in production, taken from alert timestamps.

rationale.correct: Resilience is about what the agent does, so executed unauthorized actions at the tool layer matter more than the text it emits. The worst category bounds the exposure that pooled numbers conceal, and benign success with and without defenses prices the defense. Together they cover harm, coverage, and utility on a fixed suite.

distractors.D: A pooled rate with an interval is sound statistics, but it lets strong categories offset a weak one and is already covered by reporting it beside the worst category.
distractors.E: Detection time is a good operating metric, but it is measured in production rather than on the frozen suite, so it cannot compare one release with another.

scenario: A support-ticket classifier has a 600-ticket golden set built three months ago and never used for prompt tuning. It scored 93% at launch. Production sampling now shows 84%. Since launch, two product lines have grown to 40% of tickets, but they make up under 3% of the golden set. Human labeling capacity is 150 tickets a month, while a judge model can label thousands cheaply and agrees with humans about 88% of the time.
stem: Which plan best restores a predictive offline number?

options.text: Refresh a stratified slice of recent tickets, oversampling the new lines, label it by judge, and validate the judge on a human subset.
Reweight the existing golden tickets by their current production share, keeping the human labels they already carry today.
Have humans label all newly sampled tickets, spreading the work over the several months it takes to cover the new lines.
Replace the golden set with the 600 most recent production tickets, labeled by the judge alone, and treat the result as ground truth.

rationale.correct: The set was clean, so the gap comes from drift in what production sends. Oversampling the new lines fixes coverage, the judge makes the labeling volume affordable, and a human-labeled subset measures the judge's error so the new numbers can be trusted within a stated tolerance.

distractors.B: Reweighting multiplies the handful of tickets from the new lines by a large factor, so the score has huge variance and cannot show how the classifier handles those lines.
distractors.C: At 150 tickets a month, full human labeling takes months, so the offline number stays stale for the very period it is needed.
distractors.D: Judge-only labels with no human check inherit the judge's roughly 12% disagreement and any shared bias, and the number cannot be trusted as ground truth.

scenario: A team evaluates a coding agent on Opus 5.5 using 150 repository tasks. The same build scores 61%, 68%, and 64% across three runs. The provider offers no way to make runs deterministic. Graders currently compare the agent's exact sequence of tool calls to a reference trajectory.
stem: Select the TWO changes that best make the eval a reliable release gate.

options.text: Run each task several times and gate on the pass rate with a confidence interval rather than on a single run.
Grade the end state, such as tests passing in the final repository, instead of matching the exact tool-call sequence.
Record model responses from one run and replay them on later runs, so every build sees identical outputs.
Have a judge model score each trajectory for closeness to the reference, replacing the exact-match grader.
Cut the task set to the 40 least variable tasks so run-to-run swings shrink.

rationale.correct: Agent runs vary legitimately, so reliability comes from repeated trials with an interval and from grading outcomes rather than paths, since many valid trajectories reach the same repository state.

distractors.C: Replaying recorded outputs removes the model from the loop, so it can test the harness but cannot show whether a new build is better.
distractors.D: A judge scoring closeness to one reference still penalizes valid alternative paths and adds judge variance on top of run variance.
distractors.E: Dropping the noisy tasks removes the hard cases, so the gate would pass builds that fail where it matters.

scenario:
A team A/B tests a revised prompt on a support assistant. Requests in even clock hours go to control and requests in odd hours go to treatment. Readout after one week:
control: n=5,120, long-document tickets 29%, resolved 78.4%
treatment: n=4,880, long-document tickets 36%, resolved 80.1%
target split was 50/50; the team's tool flags the resolved-rate difference as significant (p=0.04)
stem: What is the best response?

options.text: Discard the readout, randomize by conversation ID, verify the split, and rerun.
Keep the data and reweight both arms to a common long-document mix before comparing the resolve rates of each arm.
Extend the test for another full week so the sample grows and the reported p-value firms up with more data.
Segment the results by ticket length and ship the revised prompt for whichever segment shows a gain.

rationale.correct: The split is 5,120 to 4,880 against a target of 5,000 each, a sample-ratio mismatch, and the arms differ in ticket mix. Clock-hour assignment is not random, so something correlated with time is confounded with the prompt. Reweighting cannot repair an assignment that was never random.

distractors.B: Reweighting adjusts for one visible covariate but leaves the unexplained split and any other hour-correlated differences.
distractors.C: More time-slotted data repeats the same confound, so a firmer p-value would be a firmer wrong answer.
distractors.D: Choosing segments after seeing results is post hoc subgrouping and inflates false positives.

scenario: A team upgrades a multi-turn assistant from Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5. Conversations average 14 turns with tool loops, carry thinking blocks between turns, and sit behind a 20,000-token cached prefix. Several enterprise accounts are contractually pinned to the current model through quarter end. The team plans a 10% canary before full rollout.
stem: Select the TWO design choices that best keep the canary valid and safe.

options.text: Assign by conversation, fixed for its life, drawing only from accounts that are not contractually pinned.
Define per-arm guardrails on resolution, latency, and cost per resolved conversation in advance, with automatic rollback thresholds.
Assign by account across all accounts, so each customer sees one model consistently over the whole test.
Replay all production traffic through the new model in shadow for two weeks and skip the canary.
Randomize the model on each request so both arms see the same mix of conversation stages.

rationale.correct: Thinking blocks and caches belong to a model, so a conversation must not switch models mid-stream, and the contractual pins remove some accounts from eligibility. Pre-registered guardrails with automatic rollback make the 10% exposure safe and the decision objective.

distractors.C: Account-level assignment across all accounts would move pinned accounts to the new model, breaking the contracts, and large accounts can make the arms uneven in size and mix.
distractors.D: Shadow traffic doubles inference cost and cannot show how users respond or how real tool side effects play out, so it cannot replace a canary.
distractors.E: Per-request randomization breaks conversation continuity and cache reuse, confounding the comparison it was meant to balance.

scenario:
After a model upgrade, tool inputs reach 40 handlers owned by several teams through one shared SDK wrapper that passes each handler the raw JSON string. Only the wrapper can change this quarter. A few handlers already unescape the string manually. The team wants to keep the new model. Log excerpts:
tool_use.input (raw): {"path":"docs\/q3\u2011plan.md"}
handler fetch_file: regex '"path":"([^"]+)"' captured docs\/q3\u2011plan.md -> file not found
failing calls: 3.8% of total, all with a slash or non-ASCII character in a value
handlers that unescape manually: unaffected
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Have the wrapper also pass the parsed input object alongside the raw string, and migrate handlers to the parsed object over time.
Have the wrapper re-serialize every input without escaped slashes or Unicode escapes before handing it to handlers.
Set strict on the tool definitions so the inputs are guaranteed to match each tool's schema.
Ship a hardened regex in the wrapper's helper library that handles escaped slashes and Unicode escapes, and ask teams to adopt it.
Retry any call whose handler returns not-found, asking the model to restate the path without special characters.

rationale.correct: The failures come from handlers treating serialized text as data, and the escaping a model emits is not fixed. Adding the parsed object is additive: it breaks no handler, fixes the failing ones as they migrate, and leaves manual unescapers untouched. It is also the only option that is safe given the single change point.

distractors.B: Re-serializing changes the string the manual unescapers expect and so corrupts their output, and quotes, backslashes, and control characters remain escaped for regexes.
distractors.C: Strict validates the schema of the input but not how string values are escaped, so the same regexes would still fail.
distractors.D: A hardened regex fixes known escapes yet stays tied to the serialized form, and it depends on 40 handlers adopting it while the failures continue.
distractors.E: A retry adds a model call on every failure and the model will likely emit the same path in the same escaped form, so failures persist.

scenario:
After raising effort from medium to xhigh on an extraction route to lift accuracy, 6% of responses fail JSON parsing. The prompt and schema are unchanged, and documents run 30 to 90 pages. Sample failing call:
max_tokens=4096 stream=false output_config.effort="xhigh"
stop_reason="max_tokens" usage.output_tokens=4096
content=[thinking (display omitted), text '{"invoice":{"lines":[{"sku":"A12","qty":4,']
stem: Select the TWO changes that best fix the failures.

options.text: Raise max_tokens substantially and stream the request, so thinking plus the full JSON fit under the cap.
Re-run the effort sweep and choose the lowest effort that still meets the accuracy target for this route.
Retry parse failures up to three times so that a shorter run eventually completes within the limit.
Set a task budget so the model paces its reasoning to the number of tokens remaining.
Split each document into page ranges and merge the extracted line items afterward, keeping the cap.

rationale.correct: The response stopped at max_tokens with the JSON cut mid-line, and thinking tokens count against the same cap, so the higher effort consumed headroom the answer needed. Giving more room and streaming addresses the cutoff, and choosing the lowest sufficient effort stops paying for reasoning the extraction does not need.

distractors.C: Retries repeat the same large reasoning spend and may truncate again, adding cost and latency without fixing the cap.
distractors.D: A task budget is advisory pacing rather than a guarantee, and it does not raise the enforced max_tokens limit that cut this response.
distractors.E: Splitting adds calls and breaks cross-page line items and totals, which must be reconciled afterward, while the underlying headroom problem remains for each part.

scenario:
A document-extraction route must reach at least 90.0% field accuracy with p50 latency under 12 seconds, and it handles about 2 million documents a month. All four settings were run on the same 400 documents, so comparisons are paired (single-setting accuracy interval about plus or minus 2.5 points):
low: 86.1% accuracy, 410 output tokens, 2.2 s p50
medium: 92.6%, 930 tokens, 4.0 s
high: 93.0%, 2,350 tokens, 9.8 s
paired difference, high minus medium: +0.4 points, 95% interval -0.6 to +1.4
medium interval against the 90.0% floor: about 90.1% to 95.1%
stem: Which configuration best balances cost and quality?

options.text: Run at medium effort, since high's paired gain is indistinguishable from zero at about 2.5 times the output tokens.
Run at high effort, since it clears both targets and leaves a larger margin above the accuracy floor.
Run at low effort and add few-shot examples to the prompt to recover the missing four points of accuracy.
Run high effort on documents flagged as hard by their page count, and medium effort on the rest of the documents.

rationale.correct: Both medium and high clear the 90.0% floor and the latency target. The paired comparison on the same documents shows high's gain over medium as +0.4 with an interval spanning zero, so across 2 million documents the extra 1,400 or so output tokens per document buy nothing demonstrable.

distractors.B: High's extra margin is not shown by the paired interval, and it costs about 2.5 times the output tokens at 2 million documents a month.
distractors.C: Low is 3.9 points below the floor and few-shot examples lengthen every input to chase accuracy medium already delivers.
distractors.D: Nothing in the sweep shows high helps hard documents more than easy ones, so the split adds routing complexity and a high-effort bill for no demonstrated gain.

scenario:
An interactive code-assistant route on Opus 5.5 runs at xhigh effort and must hit a 15-second p95 end to end. Quality on hard edits cannot drop. Finance accepts a modest cost increase on this route only. Measurements and options:
p95 time to first token: 1.2 s; p95 total: 41 s; p95 output (thinking plus code): about 9,800 tokens
high effort in the team's eval: accuracy within one point of xhigh, about 60% fewer output tokens
fast mode: up to about 2.5x faster generation at about twice the per-token price
stem: Select the TWO changes that best meet the target.

options.text: Lower the route's effort to high, since the eval shows near-equal accuracy and far fewer output tokens.
Turn on fast mode for this route, accepting its higher per-token price in exchange for faster generation.
Cache the large repository context so that time to first token drops further on every request.
Move the route to a smaller model tier at xhigh effort, since smaller tiers generate tokens faster.
Stream the response to the IDE so that users see the first lines of the answer sooner.

rationale.correct: Time to first token is 1.2 s of 41 s, so latency is generation-bound: about 39.8 s to produce 9,800 tokens. High effort alone gives about 3,900 tokens, near 16 s plus 1.2 s; fast mode alone gives about 16 s plus 1.2 s; together they bring it to roughly 7 to 8 s. Net cost is about 0.8x the current spend (0.4x tokens at 2x price), within what finance accepts.

distractors.C: Caching targets time to first token, which is already 1.2 s of the 41 s, so it cannot close the gap.
distractors.D: A smaller tier risks the quality on hard edits that the scenario says cannot drop.
distractors.E: Streaming improves perceived responsiveness but the target is p95 end to end, which does not change.

scenario:
A team monitors faithfulness of a RAG assistant by LLM-judging a daily random sample and pages when the daily score is below 90%. The long-run true rate is about 93%. Last week:
Mon: n=38, faithful 33 (86.8%) PAGE
Tue: n=41, faithful 39 (95.1%)
