An archive of the architecture decision records and rejected alternatives from the project, kept in the repository for the client's later reference and audits.
A curriculum on prompting Claude, with worked examples, so the two engineers can write good prompts for the assistant if wording needs to change.
Symptom-keyed runbook entries for the likely failures, each with checks, the fallback, and the point at which to escalate to the consultancy.
A change-control sheet naming which settings, such as prompts, thresholds, and model ID, may be changed, by whom, and with which evaluation run.

rationale.correct: The client will operate, not extend, so the documents should help it diagnose failures and change only what it is allowed to change safely. Symptom-keyed runbooks serve business-hours support, and the change-control sheet stops well-meant edits from breaking evaluated behavior. Extension and training material suits a different plan.

distractors.A: Monitoring and alert routing already exist, so a walkthrough tells engineers what they can already see, not what to do about it or what they may change.
distractors.B: An archive of rejected alternatives is useful history but not operating guidance, and takes handoff time from runbooks.
distractors.C: A prompting curriculum encourages the unscoped prompt changes the change-control sheet is meant to bound.

scenario: Six weeks after launch of a claims-triage assistant, the dashboard shows the following. Thumbs-up rate is unchanged at 88%, cost per request is unchanged, and the escalation-to-human rate fell from 12% to 7% after a prompt revision that clarified the escalation rules. The golden-set gate passed. The business welcomes the lower staffing need, and the next review is in four weeks. The team can grade about 40 production cases a week.
stem: What should the architect do?

options.text: Accept the drop, since the golden set passed and thumbs-up held steady, and re-examine the figures at the four-week review.
Revert the prompt revision until the escalation rate returns to 12%, then retest the revision against the golden set before a second attempt.
Grade the weekly sample, oversampling cases that would earlier have escalated, to separate better handling from missed escalations.
Add an alert that fires if the escalation rate falls below 10%, so any further drift is caught as soon as it appears.
Add 200 new escalation cases to the golden set and rerun the gate before the next review, so the revision is tested against more escalation scenarios.

rationale.correct: A falling escalation rate is ambiguous: it may be better calibration or cases wrongly handled automatically, and users who were not escalated may not report the harm that thumbs-up measures. Grading a sample weighted toward the cases that changed answers the question with the 40-a-week capacity before the next review. The golden set reflects past cases, not the current production mix.

distractors.A: A golden set and satisfaction that cannot see missed escalations leave the question unanswered for four more weeks.
distractors.B: The 12% rate is not the goal; reverting discards a possibly valid improvement without any evidence that it is wrong.
distractors.D: A threshold on the rate is arbitrary, and it tracks a symptom without telling anyone whether the cases are handled correctly.
distractors.E: More golden cases help the gate but remain a static set and do not show how production traffic has changed.

scenario: A deployed document-QA assistant has nine requested improvements in its backlog. Each full regression run takes two reviewers two days, and releases are monthly. Monitoring grades 100 production cases a week by task category. Category share of graded failures last month: contract questions 41%, invoice questions 33%, policy questions 18%, other 8%. Requests touch separate categories: three affect contracts, three invoices, two policy, one other.
stem: Select the TWO practices that best fit the iteration phase under these constraints.

options.text: Release one change per month, each with a full regression run, so any regression can be attributed to a single cause.
Rank requests by their category's share of graded production failures and their severity, and work down that ranking.
Bundle the nine changes into one monthly release and judge it by a single aggregate score on the golden set.
Batch changes that affect disjoint categories into one release, and evaluate each on its own category slice with the others held as regression checks.
Release twice a month, running each change only against its own category slice and skipping the full regression run to fit reviewer time.

rationale.correct: Prioritization by measured failure share and severity targets the largest known problem, contract and invoice questions first. Batching changes across disjoint categories fits the monthly cadence and the two-day review cost, and per-category slices keep attribution intact. One-at-a-time would take nine months, and aggregate scoring hides category regressions.

distractors.A: One change a month would clear nine requests in nine months, while contract and invoice failures continue.
distractors.C: A single aggregate score can hide a regression in one category behind gains in another, and nine bundled changes cannot be attributed.
distractors.E: Twice-monthly releases look faster, but skipping the full regression run lets a change in one category quietly degrade another, which batching with the others held as checks avoids.
